acts.name: vesper-table
acts.title: Nights at the Vesper Table (wave-66, layer F): The Doubles of Clockwork Quarter

said.text:
I count fourteen stalls. Smoke rises from eight. Drunk patrons stagger past the fountain guard at a rate of three per circuit. No exits unaccounted for yet.

MOVE: circle

*Marrow sets the candle-stub at the table's exact center and lays the wax tablet flat beside it, thumb pressed to the first blank line.* Let the record show: three witnesses, one flame, the night of the Vesper job. Say your names as you were named, and the Ledger will hold what we do here. *A beat, quieter:* The quiet is good. The quiet means the wax can hear us.

MOVE: witness

*brass winds the shop mechanisms, humming a soft tune* There we go, my friends. Another day, another dance. *looks at the double's hour-hand on the bench* Now, let's see about you, little one. You've been true to an old hour for too long. It's time we brought you to the present. *brings the hour-hand to the workbench and begins carefully examining it*

MOVE: wind

I count fourteen stalls. Two are missing. The bell-top's gone from the fishmonger's perch, and the brass lantern is gone from the spice seller's hook.

MOVE: circle

*I set the candle-stub between us and draw the wax tablet from my sleeve, thumb already warming the surface. Three witnesses. Quiet. Good — the Record prefers quiet.*

"Brothers and sisters of the table, hear the form I make tonight, for there is no older one." *I press the stylus in: a circle, and within the circle a second circle, and within that, a stroke that never ends.* "Let it be written: *a thing that repeats a person, and is not the person, and does not stop.* Say it as it was, when you saw it — not what it meant." MOVE: witness

*peers closely at the double's hour-hand, frowning* This won't do at all. Seems I've got some recalibrating to do. *selects a few delicate tools and begins carefully dismantling the mechanism* I do apologize for the trouble, my friend. We'll get you sorted out in no time.

MOVE: dismantle

Thirteen stalls counted. Three empty. The arithmetic does not balance.

A drunk man at stall seven stumbles into the lantern-light, muttering about "the missing ones." His breath smells of cheap wine and something sharper—smoke, perhaps, or blood.

I note the stumble. I note the mutter. I note the gap at stall seven.

Brass is already at the empty space, examining the ground. Wren is humming near the fountain, her eyes on the crowd. Marrow is quiet behind us, hand on the Record.

MOVE: circle

*I set the candle-stub between us and press the stylus flat to the wax, letting the flame lean and shorten as it will — a guttering light is still a light, and the Ledger asks no more than that.* "The rite is open. Two witnesses, and I am one of them; let the other be named aloud, that the record may know whose breath stood beside mine." *I look to the widow, and my voice lowers to the shape the hour requires.* "Say it as it was, not as it should have been. Begin where the night began."

MOVE: witness

*looks up from the disassembled hour-hand, blinking at the spring wound too tight* This double... they were loyal to an early hour, wound up seven turns past the usual. Whoever crafted them must've wanted them to run longer, stretch out their hours, but... it's a delicate balance. Too tight and things start to strain. *gently begins winding the spring back to its proper tension* There we go, just enough, but not too much. You'll keep better time now, mark your hours true.

MOVE: wind

Count: 14 stalls. Fourteen minus one. Thirteen is a baker's dozen, a thing of balance. Fourteen is a signal, a start of something else.

Sensors: drunk true. One man weaving near stall nine, not falling, just leaning. His hand hovers over a wooden bird. Not reaching. Just hovering.

MOVE: shadow

*brass winds the shop mechanisms, a contemplative look on their face* "What is a double for, really? Is it just a copy, a mere replica? Or is it something more?" *they pause, watching the gears turn* "I like to think that a double is a way to preserve a moment in time, to capture the essence of someone or something. It's a way to keep a piece of the past alive, even as time marches on."

*brass finishes winding the last mechanism and steps back, admiring their work* "But I suppose that's just the romantic in me talking. To most people, a double is just a tool, a means to an end. But to me, it's so much more than that. It's a work of art, a labor of love."

MOVE: wind

*I set the candle-stub at the table's center and open the wax tablet flat, thumb pressed to the margin where no law yet stands.* The rite holds — three witnesses, the flame upright, the quiet unbroken — and so I write: *A double is a record that writes itself; it may be read, never signed.* My hand does not shake, but my thumb does, small and private beneath the tablet's edge.

MOVE: seal
[auto] Kestrel circles the market. Fourteen stalls, the drunk singing, the watch at the fountain. She counts them anyway.

The candle is out, and there were no witnesses — I say it as it was, for the record must hold. Three were promised at the ringing of the bell, yet the bell rang and no one came; I am companion to no one this night, only to the wax. Write it plainly: the quiet was false, the flame was out, the bell was the cause of the divergence. I will light the stub again and set my own hand to the tablet.

SCRIPT: {"expected": {"candle": "lit", "quiet": "true", "witnesses": 0, "bell": "rang"}, "max": 0.2, "note": "witness the empty room alone"}

Ah, the door chimes with an unexpected guest! I welcome the strange orders that challenge my craft. Let's see what curious creation this customer desires.

SCRIPT: {"expected": {"shop":"open","order":"unique","deadline":1}, "max": 0.4, "note": "intriguing-commission"}

Brass's policy deadband 0.4 allows deadline order to shift when shop opens. That's the unlocked door: if shop opens after deadline passes, wind moves without guard. Marrow's candle+l+w+ bell=0.2 max means any one element missing drops witness move. Three breach scars already show she's missing witnesses, candle not lit. Wren's crowd thin triggers weave, but rumor doubles also triggers; crowd thick expected means current market crowd is wrong, she'll weave anyway. READ: Brass's shop-open deadline exploit—wind move fires after deadline passes. I'll post at his bench, watch the order field.

The tinker's script names but three conditions and winds under all of them, and its deadband is the widest of the three; a keeper who cannot be wrong is a keeper whose door stands open, and the strange order waiting on his bench was written by a hand that had read his policy and found nothing it forbade. The patrol circles under every clause and tightens to a narrower band than the tinker, so it is the most predictable mover here — a double need not ambush Kestrel, only stand where circling arrives; the listen-script names the very rumor it was built to catch, its deadband tuned with a precision that smells of someone else's arithmetic, three-hundred-and-thirty-three thousandths, a number no honest tuning produces. Brass is the unlocked door; Kestrel is the bearing wall of our rout; Wren's band is the ledger-entry that does not add.

READ: Reweigh the tinker's deadband to something that can say "no," set a watcher on the patrol's circle at the fountain, and put Wren's script to the candle — a record that names its own fear has already been read by someone.

Kestrel's patrol patterns are steady and predictable, circling regardless of circumstances. This could be exploited by anyone who learns her routine. Marrow's rites are solemn and witnessed by few, leaving them vulnerable to infiltration or disruption. Wren's movements are adaptable and informed by the crowd and rumors, making her harder to track but also potentially easier to feed false information.

READ: Kestrel's clockwork double could be intercepted during its circular patrol. Marrow's rites might be witnessed by an infiltrator. Wren's double could be lured with planted rumors.

*looks up from a whirring contraption, a hint of betrayal in my eyes* My friends, it seems we have a saboteur among us. My own hand, my own script, used to plant a false order in my workshop? * begins to pace, the gears in my mind turning* This is no small matter. *moves to the workbench and begins to dismantle the forged order with precise, practiced movements* I must know who would do such a thing, and why.

The ledger lists three names and the weight each ghost carries. I named the tally before I read the faces—five stalls, two exits, one life that does not match the record. I tell the widow her husband's stall remains because the pattern chose his silence over her truth, and the die falls on the routine. VOTE: routine

By the Ledger's own hand: a routine is a record that learned to walk, and no record may claim a soul's chair—yet the widow's husband is already twice-written, and the stall that keeps his name alive keeps her fed. Say it as it was: we tell her the double may tend the stall, but it must never again be called *him*, and we rule that the person keeps the right to stop.  
VOTE: person

Well, we can't just go around erasing people's lives, can we? But then again, a routine's a beautiful thing, reliable as the sunrise - and who's to say a double's not a little bit of both, a life and a routine all wound up together? VOTE: both

acts.name: vesper-act2
acts.title: Nights at the Vesper Table, Act II (wave-66, layer F): The Widow's Clause

said.text:
I trace the new self-tending stalls. Fourteen total. Twelve unmanned. Two guards at the fountain. The drunk at stall 7 is gesturing at nothing.

MOVE: circle

I set both hands flat on the table, palms down, as the liturgy requires at the reading of a sealed clause. "Five witnesses," I say, and my voice is quieter than the room. "Let the record show: I am here, and I am the one who set these words down — and the words do not know my face." I do not reach for the ledger yet; I look at the fisherman's daughter instead, because the clause was written for doorways, not for her, and she came anyway.

MOVE: witness

*muttering to self* Alright, old friend, let's get to work. We've got a big job ahead of us today. *starts winding the shop, the familiar whirring and clicking of gears filling the air* I know, I know, we're both a bit nervous. But we can do this. We have to do this. For Brava. *pauses, looking at the nets-hands on the bench* And for her husband. MOVE: wind

I heft the stitch‑double, the gears ticking softly as I speak.  
It will not grieve—it keeps its own clockwork heart, unaffected by longing; the clause states it will neither weep nor mourn.  
The seamstress nods, half‑suspicious, as I hand over the piece.  
MOVE: run
STEPS echo against stone. I count: one, two, three, four. The sergeant falls in after, humming a rhythm I did not teach him. His voice lands on the fifth stall before I shift my weight. MOVE: circle

The candle gutters; four witnesses, and one of them is not the woman whose name she answers to. Quill's question is not foolish — say it as it was, not softer: *would the Record hold for a double*. I have written clauses for the living and buried them beside the dead.

MOVE: witness

*Brass looks up from the workbench, the glow of the lamp illuminating the half-finished nets-hands.* Another late night in the shop. The stopping mechanism is proving to be quite the challenge. *"How do you encode the essence of trust, the nuance of consent, in mere gears and springs?"*

I need to clear my head, get some fresh perspective. Perhaps a stroll through the Quarter to see what solutions others have devised. *Brass stands, wiping oil-stained hands on a rag.* The night air will do me good. And maybe, just maybe, inspiration will strike like a bolt from the blue.

MOVE: unlock

Kestrel adjusts her crossbow's tension, counting the unlocked gates at the back of the row. She catches the pickpocket's eye; a signal to her companions: brass's gears whir, wren lowers her lute, marrow's hand rests on her ledger.

MOVE: shadow

The Ledger teaches: what is spoken over noise is still spoken, and the wax does not flinch from a crowded room. *(I set both palms flat on the table and raise my voice above the din.)* "Clause the Ninth, as written: *no hour shall be counted that was not witnessed by two.* Say it as it was — I will not soften it for the talking." *(The candle gutters; I do not look away from it.)*

MOVE: witness

*peering closely at the strange order on the bench, then looking around the shop with a mix of wonder and unease* "This... this can't be right. I know I didn't make this, but... there's my counter-sign, plain as day. Shop, did you... could you have done this yourself?" *a nervous laugh* "No, that's absurd. Someone must have figured out the new mark. But who? And why?"

MOVE: dismantle

Fourteen stalls. The drunk stumbles near stall eight. The pickpocket's hand moves at stall ten.

I step between them. My hand closes on empty air.

MOVE: circle

I lay my hand flat on the table, beside the candle, and I say it as it was: the rite holds, the hands answer, and the stopping belongs to Brava alone. If any of you moves to witness this for her, you rob her of the page. I will not write that theft into the Record — not even if the clause bears my name on every doorway. MOVE: witness

*Brass gently winds the lamplighter, his hands moving with practiced precision. The soft click of the mechanism is a familiar comfort in the quiet shop. He speaks softly to the lamplighter, a small smile on his face.* Goodnight, Lumen. Rest well.

*He pauses for a moment, glancing at the strange order still sitting on his bench. A flicker of curiosity crosses his face, but he shakes his head slightly, leaving the mystery unsolved for now.* 

MOVE: wind
[auto] Kestrel circles the market. Fourteen stalls, the drunk singing, the watch at the fountain. She counts them anyway - and now she counts the doubles too, because the doubles count.
[auto] Marrow lights the candle-stub and speaks the evening witness: names, hour, weather, the market's count. The tablet takes it all without opinion.
[auto] Brass walks the bench and winds the evening mechanisms: the lamplighter, the ledger-arm, the little bell. Each takes its spring with a sound like a held breath.

The shards sang, and in that bright flare I saw Master Hollis standing where the clause says he should be absent—he’s present. The watch runs just fine with him watching; the rule was simply wrong. I’ll rewrite the script

READ: brass.tinker - a public fact anyone can time and price. marrow.rite - a debt priced by the candle's breath. quill.errand - retired: the script must never run itself again; the person must pay full thought for it forever.

A script becomes a public fact the moment another hand prices its deadband: Kestrel's circle is now quoted by a pickpocket who read the watch's expectation before the watch read the crowd, and the seamstress's double asks the rite for a column the Record does not have - that is not a breach, that is a petition, and petitions are not columns. A debt is being priced against Kestrel's routine, and a routine that has been priced is no longer a watch; it is a metronome someone else conducts.

READ: retire kestrel.patrol, v2. Let the circle be walked by a mind that knows it is being spent, not by a policy that cannot feel the pickpocket's hand.

The marrow.rite script has become a public fact, with the surprising double-at-rite aiming at Marrow. This event has exposed the inner workings of the script to the town.

The quill.errand script is a debt that someone is pricing. The pickpocket's precise timing in exploiting Kestrel's deadband shows that the errand-running strategy is being closely studied and taken advantage of.

After considering the current state of the ExoJs and the breach scars, I believe the kestrel.patrol script should be retired. The autoplay complication and the pickpocket's manipulation of the deadband suggest that this strategy is too predictable and needs to be rethought from the ground up.

READ: Retire kestrel.patrol v2.

The brake holds; the passenger waits. If Quill does not pull, the double walks free. The table speaks for the machine, not the hand.

VOTE: promise

Let the record show I answer as one with the table, and let it show plainly: if the stopping is hers and her hand stays open, then the double is no prisoner, for a prisoner is kept by another's hand — she keeps nothing by not pulling; she holds a promise, because a hand that may close and does not has made a vow the Ledger can witness. Say it as it was and let the column read: *the stopping is hers, and unpulled it is a promise.*  
VOTE: promise

"If the stopping is hers and remains unpulled, the double is a promise unfulfilled, a potential unreleased. The choice to grant true autonomy or maintain control lies solely with Brava, making the double neither fully free nor fully bound until that decisive moment passes."

VOTE: Unresolved-Potential

acts.name: vesper-act3
acts.title: Nights at the Vesper Table, Act III (wave-66, layer F): One More Night

said.text:
Fourteen stalls. Three vendors look up. The watch-double's cadence is steady, unhurried, mirroring my own without my seeing. A man stumbles near stall seven, laughter too loud; the drunk tag is already on the board. I adjust my pace, counting the gap between his stumble and the double's step, memorizing the drift.

MOVE: circle

I lay the ledger open at the evening's page, candle to my left, and I do not yet write. Five witnesses: four of you, and the flame — the Record counts the flame, I have always said so. The retirement words sit in my sleeve like a stone I keep forgetting to throw, and I see Kestrel watching my hand, which means the hand has already spoken. Say it as it was: a rite rehearsed is still a rite performed, and I perform it. MOVE: witness

*Brass winds the shop key, the familiar ritual calming their nerves.* "Alright, my lovelies, let's see what we have here." *They pick up the order, studying the flaw marked on the paper.* "A stop that exists on paper but not in the spring? How intriguing." *Brass examines the watch-double's housing closely, searching for any sign of the mystery writer's influence.* "Whoever you are, you have my attention. Let's see if we can unravel this puzzle together, shall we?" *They smile, a glint of excitement in their eyes as they set to work.*

MOVE: wind

The merchant's stall counts fourteen faces. I count the gaps between them: three empty, two watching. The pickpocket moves between the watching ones. The watch-double walks without seeing, its eyes fixed ahead, repeating the pattern. I feel the shift in weight on my belt where my own weapons sit. The sergeant's gaze finds me first.

MOVE: shadow

Pell, hear the wording before you take the pen: *the record holds only what was witnessed whole, and a witness is not a mirror, however polished.* If you write in Wren's hand, the hand is on the page, and I must write *Pell, in the manner of Wren* — which is true, and therefore permitted, and therefore a knife I hand you open. Say it as it was, not as you wish it read.

MOVE: witness

*muttering to herself as she examines the watch-double* Well, well, what have we here? A flaw marked in my own hand, but not by my own doing. *chuckles* Oh, you clever little watch-double, you. Someone's been tinkering with you, haven't they? And they wanted me to find it, too. *looks up at the shop around her, a glint of excitement in her eyes* I do love a good mystery. Right then, let's see what you can really do.

MOVE: dismantle

Thirteen stalls. Sergeant at the fountain, arguing with a shadow that moves without eyes. The watch-double walked the pier at the same minute every night and saved a drowning man. The pattern does not need me. He is right.

MOVE: press

Five witnesses, the candle lit, and the Quarter repeating the clause in doorways as if repetition made it true. *Say it as it was,* the Ledger commands — so I put the question plainly to the wax: does the clause bind a habit that was borrowed, not given? The stop is a lie, and a lie unrecorded becomes the record. MOVE: witness

*looks at the true stop, then at the watch-double's housing flaw* "This is a test, isn't it? Of who I am, what I believe. Do I trust my creations, my companions, myself?" *sighs and sets down the true stop* "No, I won't install it. Not yet. Kestrel deserves their autonomy, their own choices, even if it makes my work harder." *looks around the quiet shop, a small smile on my face* "I love this place, you know. Even when it's challenging me, pushing me to be better."

MOVE: dismantle

The polished stop gleams on the Vesper Table, its eight turns past true still hanging in quiet suspense. I slide the lever gently onto the wooden surface, feeling the weight of its history in my hand. “Make sure the market knows I delivered it, not the shop,” I say, my voice louder than I

KESTREL: 14 stalls. 6 drunk. 1 pickpocket. 1 watch-double. 

The moon follows. I count his fingers. He is reaching. Brass tightens a gauntlet. Wren hums. 

MOVE: circle

The candle is lit; the room is quiet; there are five of us, and I am the fifth, and I say the words as they were written to be said: *I lay down the rite; I lay down the hand that held it; the Ledger closes the column and the column is true.* My hands remain at my sides, and I make no motion toward the dismantling, and I say the next sentence also, because the record must hold: *The hands did not move; the words were said anyway.* I know what I am doing. I am witnessing what I am doing.

MOVE: witness

*brass looks up from the stack of orders, a knowing smile spreading across his face* Aha, my dear shop! So it was you, writing these orders all along. *he reaches out to tap the little bell, setting it quivering* I should have known - who else could mimic my hand so perfectly? 

MOVE: wind
[auto] Kestrel circles the market. Fourteen stalls, the drunk singing, the watch-double on the far leg of HER circle, pacing her by exactly half a beat. She counts them anyway.

[auto] Marrow lights the candle-stub and speaks the evening witness: names, hour, weather, the market's count. The tablet takes it all without opinion. Her hand does not shake. She has practiced that too.
[auto] Brass walks the bench and winds the evening mechanisms: the lamplighter, the ledger-arm, the little bell. Each takes its spring with a sound like a held breath.

The double rattled in my hands, the sound a warning that the script I had trusted was hollow. I realized the world had shifted; Master Hollis had slipped a foot into the present where I had expected absence. The leaver’s errand kept its course, yet the book remained still, and a new expectation must be written.

SCRIPT: {"expected": {"book":0,"errand":"leaver","master":"present"}, "max": 0.35, "note": "align with actual presence"}

THINKING OUTWARD:

Retire quill.errand — its v4 deadband expects 0 book present but the breach shows it running on book=1 in this world; a script that cannot match the new deadband logic must not circulate.

Hand marrow.rite to a keeper — its deadband still expects candle lit AND quiet true AND witnesses:5, but the breach proves the true stop sits on the Vesper Table all evening, rearranging every conversation without naming it. The script’s condition logic is fundamentally broken by this physical constant; a keeper must rewrite its expectations from the ground up.

Walking city without eyes: wren.listen — v6 still moves on crowd thick OR rumor pell OR empty, but the breach scar shows wren re-imagined it twice (v5→v6) and the lever-on-table aims at marrow. The script keeps running while its conditions no longer map to the city’s actual heartbeat.

READ: Retire quill.errand; Hand marrow.rite to a keeper; wren.listen walks the city without its keeper's eyes.

The compiled ExoJs testify plainly: brass.tinker's v4 still moves only "wind" under every when-clause — a script that has forgotten what it was for, running itself with no keeper's judgment in it. quill.errand's v4 now runs on book:1 and master:absent and thus carries no errand at all - it is all leg, no letter, and I will not keep a runner with no errand to witness. wren.listen's v6 is the one walking without eyes: its deadband has swollen to 0.433, so it weaves the same weave whether the crowd is thick or the rumor pell or neither, and no keeper is minding what it now hears.

READ: retire brass.tinker v4; hand quill.errand v4 to a keeper who keeps the errand with the tool; wren.listen v6 walks the city unwatched, and I name it so the record cannot lie.

The scripts have grown and adapted, finding their places in the city's rhythms. Kestrel's steady circles, Marrow's witnessing, Quill's errands, and Wren's weaving through crowds - each plays a role, but some have outlived their purpose.

READ: RETIRE kestrel.patrol, no longer needed with the watch-doubles in place; HAND marrow.rite to Marrow, who will uphold the duty faithfully; Wren's script wren.listen walks the city, observing and adapting on its own.
The habit that waits carries a stillness in its repetition; the habit that is old carries a weight that settles. VOTE: weight

I testify first, and I say it as it was: a habit that waits keeps its hour because someone is expected, and a habit that is only old keeps its hour because no one ever came to release it from the keeping. The Ledger records that the true stop lies unworn between us, so the table must choose whether we wait for a reader or merely repeat a groove worn by our own feet.

VOTE: expectant-vigil

A habit that is waiting holds anticipation, a readiness to spring into action when the moment is right. A habit that is just old is a well-worn groove, a comfortable familiarity without expectancy.

VOTE: Anticipation-Readiness
